Milcah
MIL-kah
proper noun
Hebrew Milcah, “queen” or “counsel,” one of the five daughters of Zelophehad of the tribe of Manasseh.

Biblical Definition

Milcah was one of the five daughters of Zelophehad the son of Hepher, of the family of Manasseh the son of Joseph (Num 26:33). She must be distinguished from the earlier Milcah, the daughter of Haran and wife of Nahor, Abraham’s brother, who bore him eight sons and was grandmother of Rebekah (Gen 11:29; 22:20–23); the two are different women, and only the name is shared. This Milcah of Manasseh, with her sisters Mahlah, Noah, Hoglah, and Tirzah, came before Moses and the congregation when their father died without sons in the wilderness, and sought a possession among their father’s brethren that his name be not done away (Num 27:1–4). The LORD declared their cause just, and gave them an inheritance (Num 27:7). When the heads of the fathers of the tribe of Gilead feared that the daughters’ marriage outside the tribe might carry their portion away, the LORD ordered that they marry within the family of their father, that no inheritance pass from tribe to tribe (Num 36:1–9). Milcah obeyed and married within the families of Manasseh (Num 36:11). She stands among the daughters who, by faith and in submission to the LORD’s appointed order, both received their inheritance in the land and kept it within the covenant bounds He set.

Webster 1828 Definition

One of the five daughters of Zelophehad; not the Milcah, wife of Nahor, of Genesis, but a daughter of Manasseh.

MILCAH, one of the five daughters of Zelophehad (Num 26:33).

She is distinct from Milcah, wife of Nahor, in Genesis (Gen 11:29).

Her father, of Manasseh, died without sons.

She and her sisters sought and received an inheritance (Num 27:7).

She married within the families of Manasseh (Num 36:11).

Key Scripture

Num 26:33 — "And Zelophehad the son of Hepher had no sons, but daughters: and the names of the daughters of Zelophehad were Mahlah, and Noah, Hoglah, Milcah, and Tirzah."

Num 27:1 — "Then came the daughters of Zelophehad, the son of Hepher, the son of Gilead, the son of Machir, the son of Manasseh, of the families of Manasseh the son of Joseph: and these are the names of his daughters; Mahlah, Noah, and Hoglah, and Milcah, and Tirzah."

Num 36:11 — "For Mahlah, Tirzah, and Hoglah, and Milcah, and Noah, the daughters of Zelophehad, were married unto their father's brothers' sons:"

Gen 11:29 — "And Abram and Nahor took them wives: the name of Abram's wife was Sarai; and the name of Nahor's wife, Milcah, the daughter of Haran, the father of Milcah, and the father of Iscah."

Modern Corruption

A figure of Scripture, not a contested doctrine; she witnesses that God’s daughters receive their portion within His covenant order.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the petition of Zelophehad’s daughters was not a demand for autonomy but a request made in faith and in order, granted by God within the law of inheritance and bounded by the requirement to marry within their tribe (Num 36). Milcah of Manasseh is sometimes pressed into a modern tale of women claiming rights against an order; the text shows instead a daughter who sought the preservation of her father’s name, received her portion by the LORD’s judgment, and married within her tribe as His law required.

The chief difficulty this entry must clear is not a culture war but a confusion of names: this Milcah is not the wife of Nahor in Genesis, though they share the name. The careful reader honours Scripture by keeping its persons distinct. And in keeping Milcah of Manasseh in her own story, we see again the harmony of God’s law, which gives the inheritance to the faithful daughter and yet guards the inheritance of the tribe — categories of covenant and order, not of autonomy and grievance.

Hebrew Roots

The name means “queen” or “counsel,” borne by a daughter of Zelophehad and, distinctly, by the wife of Nahor.
